extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy/epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing John Locke's account of the origin of ideas (Book II, Chapter I): his empiricist claim that all ideas derive from sensation or reflection, his critique of innate principles, and related claims about perception, consciousness, and the development of ideas in children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge depends on right use of faculties, not innate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: OUR KNOWLEDGE DEPENDS UPON THE RIGHT USE OF THOSE POWERS NATURE HATH BESTOWED UPON US, and how little upon SUCH INNATE PRINCIPLES AS ARE IN VAIN SUPPOSED TO BE IN ALL MANKIND.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples: many truths (e.g., triangle angles) are evident but unknown to millions who never exercised the relevant faculties; thus knowledge accrues by employing faculties to discover and retain truths rather than by assuming innate ideas. Anti-pattern: accepting doctrines on trust as 'innate' instead of examining them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men must think and know for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth has been my only aim; and wherever that has appeared to lead, my thoughts have impartially followed, without minding whether the footsteps of any other lay that way or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for inquiry: prioritize direct consideration of things themselves and use one's own reasoning rather than relying on authority or 'reverend names'. Example contrast: Aristotle's reputation did not rest on his uncritical adoption of others' views. Anti-pattern: 'taking up another’s principles, without examining them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion of innate principles (principles must be examined)
rubrics_metrics.description: When men have found some general propositions that could not be doubted as soon as understood, it was a short and easy way to conclude them innate... that there are innate principles, it put their followers upon a necessity of receiving SOME doctrines as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative rule: treat supposed 'innate' truths skeptically; investigate how purported universal truths actually arose (often from consideration of things themselves). Warning: labeling propositions 'innate' can be used to shut down inquiry and enforce authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: All ideas come from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: To this I answer, in one word, from EXPERIENCE. In that all our knowledge is founded; and from that it ultimately derives itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core empirical claim: appeal to observation and personal experience as the ultimate source of the materials of thought. Use this as a test for claims about origins of ideas: ask what experience could have produced them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fountains of ideas: Sensation and Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: These two are the fountains of knowledge, from whence all the ideas we have, or can naturally have, do spring: external sensible objects (SENSATION) and the operations of our own minds (REFLECTION).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic framework: categorize any idea as deriving from (a) sensation—perceptions caused by external objects, or (b) reflection—perception of the mind's own operations. Use this taxonomy to trace the origin of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation furnishes ideas of sensible qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Senses, conversant about particular sensible objects, do convey into the mind several distinct perceptions of things... IDEAS we have of yellow, white, heat, cold, soft, hard, bitter, sweet, and all those which we call sensible qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical identification: sensible qualities (colors, tastes, tactile properties, temperatures, etc.) should be attributed to sensory experience. Example: color and taste concepts derive from bodily contact with objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection furnishes ideas of the mind’s operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The perception of the operations of our own mind within us... do furnish the understanding with another set of ideas... such as perception, thinking, doubting, believing, reasoning, knowing, willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical identification: introspective awareness of mental acts yields concepts like belief, doubt, willing. These are not derived from external objects but from observing one's own mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: All ideas are from one of the two sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding seems to me not to have the least glimmering of any ideas which it doth not receive from one of these two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic rule: when confronted with a supposed idea, test whether it can plausibly be traced to sensation or reflection; if not, suspect confusion or an unwarranted claim of innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas are acquired gradually and observable in children
rubrics_metrics.description: He that attentively considers the state of a child, at his first coming into the world, will have little reason to think him stored with plenty of ideas... It is BY DEGREES he comes to be furnished with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical test: developmental observations support empiricism—infants gain ideas over time as they encounter sensory input and reflect. Example: a child kept only among black and white would not acquire ideas of scarlet or green.

rubrics_metrics.name: People differ in their ideas according to what they converse with
rubrics_metrics.description: Men then come to be furnished with fewer or more simple ideas from without, according as the objects they converse with afford greater or less variety; and from the operations of their minds within, according as they more or less reflect on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory principle: diversity of knowledge across people is explained by differences in experience and attentiveness. Implication: evaluation of someone's knowledge should consider their experiential exposure and reflective habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection requires attention and develops later
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of Reflection later, because they need Attention... unless he turn his thoughts that way, and considers them ATTENTIVELY, he will no more have clear and distinct ideas of all the operations of his mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological advice: to form clear ideas of one's own mental operations one must deliberately attend inwardly; without attentive reflection such ideas remain confused. Pedagogical implication: teach introspective skills to develop reflective concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Having ideas is the same as perceiving
rubrics_metrics.description: To ask, at what TIME a man has first any ideas, is to ask, when he begins to perceive;—HAVING IDEAS, and PERCEPTION, being the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual clarification: equate the occurrence of ideas with the onset of perception; questions about when ideas begin reduce to when perception begins (useful when discussing infancy or the soul).

rubrics_metrics.name: No proof the soul always thinks; be critical of metaphysical assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: But whether the soul be supposed to exist antecedent to... I leave to be disputed... I confess myself to have one of those dull souls, that doth not perceive itself always to contemplate ideas; nor can conceive it any more necessary for the soul always to think, than for the body always to move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic caution: avoid asserting metaphysical necessities (e.g., 'the soul always thinks') without empirical grounds; rely on experience where possible. Anti-pattern: defining the soul into properties (circular definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is essential to counting as thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The perception of ideas being... to the soul, what motion is to the body; not its essence, but one of its operations... I am afraid, is to be sure without proofs... Consciousness is the perception of what passes in a man’s own mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for thinking: thinking entails conscious awareness; claims of unconscious thinking should be scrutinized since they entail paradoxes (e.g., making 'two persons' of one man). Use waking/sleep examples to test claims about consciousness and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that the soul thinks during non-dreaming sleep are implausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Most men, I think, pass a great part of their sleep without dreaming... To suppose the soul to think, and the man not to perceive it, is... to make two persons in one man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative standard: when evaluating theories that posit unconscious thinking (e.g., soul-thinking in sleep), demand evidence and consider the absurd consequences (lack of memory, multiplicity of persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams mostly reorganize waking ideas; do not prove native ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The dreams of sleeping men are, as I take it, all made up of the waking man’s ideas; though for the most part oddly put together... It is strange the soul should never once in a man’s whole life recall over any of its pure native thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive rule: treat dreams as recombinations of previously acquired (sensory/reflected) ideas rather than as access to innate, independent ideas. Use dream content as evidence about source of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and retention argue against disembodied thinking without impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: It will perhaps be said... that the soul in a sleeping man thinks apart, and making no use of the organs of the body, leaves no impressions on it, and consequently no memory of such thoughts... Whatever ideas the mind can receive and contemplate without the help of the body, it is reasonable to conclude it can retain without the help of the body too; or else the soul... will have but little advantage by thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating theories of mind: require an account of how thoughts could be retained and made useful absent bodily impressions; otherwise the hypothesis is inefficient or implausible. Anti-pattern: positing thinking that leaves no trace or use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation of fetuses and infants supports empiricism
rubrics_metrics.description: Infants newly come into the world spend the greatest part of their time in sleep... a Fœtus in the mother’s womb differs not much from the state of a vegetable... where the eyes have no light, and the ears so shut up are not very susceptible of sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical grounding: use developmental and physiological observations (e.g., fetal environment) to argue that perceptual experience is necessary for ideas to form; this undermines claims of pre-birth innate ideas.
